{"id": "79:28/q04", "question": "What does fa-sawwaha mean?", "turns_on": "Whether taswiya concerns a seamless surface, completed construction, proportion and wise order, or the placement and furnishing of individual celestial bodies.", "positions": [{"id": "79:28/q04/p1", "position": "God made the sky even and seamless, without disparities, cracks, or flaws.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī specifies no high or low part and even height and extent; Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī mention a smooth surface without rises or depressions. Muqātil, Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Baghawī, Ibn Jawzī, Qurtubī, Nasafī, Biqāʿī, and Study Quran emphasize absence of flaws, seams, breaks, fissures, or unequal elevation. Rāzī's reported view and Study Quran link this to 67:3, the latter also to 67:4. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ accepts this as a possible close sense."}, {"id": "79:28/q04/p2", "position": "God completed, perfected, and set the sky right as its construction required.", "reasons": "Kashshāf gives this alongside smoothness; Rāzī reports composing and proportioning it; Bayḍāwī says the verb can mean setting right. Abū Ḥayyān gives perfected construction; Ibn Kathīr adds leveling and adornment with stars. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ accepts completion, repair, and precise construction as textually possible."}, {"id": "79:28/q04/p3", "position": "God proportioned and ordered the sky and its parts according to wisdom.", "reasons": "Jishumī defines taswiya as matching one thing to another in form and meaning. Biqāʿī says the thicknesses of each heaven and earth and the spaces between them were proportioned so none exceeds another. Ālūsī says each part received what wisdom requires, including stars; Elmalılı cites 55:7 on the balance. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says each part was arranged in its right place and compares 38:72. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ stresses straightness, balance, equilibrium, and precision; Asad says 87:2 is the earliest chronological use of sawwā in this sense."}, {"id": "79:28/q04/p4", "position": "God completed the sky by furnishing it with stars, celestial spheres, and epicycles.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī gives stars, spheres, and other features as an explanation. Ālūsī reports the version with stars, accessories, and epicycles but objects that it identifies heavens with spheres without early support and rests on weak astronomical proofs; he leaves the truth to God."}, {"id": "79:28/q04/p5", "position": "God placed each heavenly body in its proper position.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ attributes this to Muḥammad ʿAbduh but rejects it as a poor fit for the Qur'anic sense of evenness and precision."}]}
{"id": "79:28/q05", "question": "Does taswiya establish that the sky is spherical?", "turns_on": "Whether unqualified proportion requires a sphere, or leaves the sky's overall shape undetermined.", "positions": [{"id": "79:28/q05/p1", "position": "Complete proportion implies a genuinely spherical sky.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports advocates arguing that the unqualified wording requires complete proportion: other shapes have edges and unequal distances, while sphericity causes no religious harm. Ālūsī reports many scholars held that the heavens have simple, similar parts and a genuinely spherical form; their dependence on a freely choosing creator makes this religiously unobjectionable."}, {"id": "79:28/q05/p2", "position": "The wording does not establish the sky's overall shape.", "reasons": "Elmalılı rejects the inference to a perfect sphere and says the detail is known to God."}]}
{"id": "79:28/q06", "question": "How does this statement relate to the preceding mention of building the sky?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:28/q06/p1", "position": "It explains how God built the sky.", "reasons": "Rāzī says the passage turns from stating that God built heaven to explaining its manner. Samīn says raising its height explains that manner, and Bursevī says the vast rise from earth does so."}]}
{"id": "79:28/q07", "question": "How does this verse's creation sequence relate to Fussilat's sequence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:28/q07/p1", "position": "An apparent conflict is alleged: Fussilat puts earth's creation before heaven, while this passage puts heaven's construction before earth's spreading.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba reports the objection, citing 41:9 and 41:12 against 79:27, 79:28, and 79:30; the note gives no resolution."}]}
{"id": "79:28/q08", "question": "What does the sky's creation show in the sura's argument?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:28/q08/p1", "position": "Its vast, ordered creation demonstrates God's power to resurrect people.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī places the signs within the sura's purpose of establishing resurrection, gathering, and final fate after earlier suras' exposition; its oaths signal a decisive climax. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the question makes deniers answer for themselves: recreating decayed bones is no harder than making the sky. Kur'an Yolu calls the vast ordered cosmos evidence to resurrection deniers, citing 40:57, and treats pillarless heavens as a sign of limitless power, citing 13:2; it also includes night and day, citing 2:164 and 78:10–11. Study Quran includes the sky, night and day, and spread earth as dimensions of creation showing power to create and resurrect."}]}
{"id": "79:31/q01", "question": "How is 'He brought forth' connected to the preceding account of spreading the earth?", "turns_on": "Whether the unjoined clause explains the preceding verb, supplies a circumstance with implied qad, or functions as a substitution of inclusion.", "positions": [{"id": "79:31/q01/p1", "position": "It explains or details what spreading the earth entails, so no conjunction is needed.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, as reported by al-Samīn, says spreading prepared earth for habitation and this clause details the water and provisions required for settlement. Rāzī adds food and stabilizing mountains; Bursevī calls the clause an explanation or completion of preparation. Ālūsī likewise says livelihood requires food and drink. Al-Kashshāf and Bayḍāwī present this as one of two analyses."}, {"id": "79:31/q01/p2", "position": "It is an unjoined circumstantial clause, with an implicit qad: the earth was spread while its water and pasture were brought forth.", "reasons": "Rāzī states the simultaneous circumstance. Qurṭubī and al-Samīn cite the analogous construction at 4:90; al-Samīn calls supplying qad the majority analysis and says Kufans and al-Akhfash oppose it. Al-Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī, and Ālūsī also give this analysis as an alternative."}, {"id": "79:31/q01/p3", "position": "It is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from 'He spread it.'", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the two verbs have different meanings and the earth's useful contents complete its spreading."}, {"id": "79:31/q01/p4", "position": "The verb appears without a coordinating conjunction; this note gives no further construction.", "reasons": "Nasafī expressly observes the absence of a conjunction before akhraja."}]}
{"id": "79:31/q02", "question": "What water is brought out of the earth?", "turns_on": "Which forms of earthly water the general phrase specifies: springs, rivers, seas, their combination, or water issuing from within earth without further specification.", "positions": [{"id": "79:31/q02/p1", "position": "The earth's gushing springs.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf, Ibn al-Jawzī, Rāzī, Qurṭubī, Bayḍāwī, and Nasafī describe springs issuing or gushing from the earth."}, {"id": "79:31/q02/p2", "position": "Springs and flowing rivers.", "reasons": "Ālūsī says God opened springs and caused rivers to flow. Elmalılı also speaks of creation, gushing springs, and flowing rivers. Ṭabāṭabāʾī names released springs and rivers."}, {"id": "79:31/q02/p3", "position": "Rivers made to flow.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī states this directly and transmits it from al-Ḍaḥḥāk; al-Suyūṭī transmits Ibn Jurayj's same gloss."}, {"id": "79:31/q02/p4", "position": "Seas, rivers, springs, and all water.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī transmits Ibn ʿAbbās naming seas, rivers, springs, and all water. Ṭabrisī transmits Ibn ʿAbbās naming rivers, seas, and springs."}, {"id": "79:31/q02/p5", "position": "Water belonging within the earth and emerging from it, without specifying a waterbody.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī infers an internal origin from the possessive attribution 'its water.' Bursevī says water is attributed to earth because it emerges from it."}, {"id": "79:31/q02/p6", "position": "The earth's seas.", "reasons": "Muqātil identifies its water as seas, since they come from the earth."}]}
{"id": "79:31/q03", "question": "Why is water mentioned before pasture?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:31/q03/p1", "position": "Water causes the pasture to grow.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports Abū Ḥayyān's explanation that the order follows the causal dependence of pasture on water."}]}
{"id": "79:31/q04", "question": "What do water and pasture together stand for?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:31/q04/p1", "position": "They encompass the earth's provisions and benefits for people and animals.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba and his later transmitters enumerate grass, trees, grain, fruit or dates, chaff or straw, leaves, wood or fuel, clothing, fire from wood, and salt from water; Rāzī also names medicine, says worldly pleasures stem from water and plants, and cites 21:30, 56:71–72, and 2:25. Ṭabrisī says water sustains animals, trees, fruit, grain, and springs, while pasture supplies livestock. Ibn ʿĀshūr includes cooking fuel and salt, and argues that mention of pasture suffices for fruit and grain because care for animals implies still greater care for people; he cites 79:33 for the ellipsis. Ālūsī says settlement requires food and drink."}]}
{"id": "79:31/q05", "question": "What does 'its pasture' denote here?", "turns_on": "Whether marʿā here is limited to grazed fodder, includes human food too, or alludes to plant life generally; notes also discuss its verbal-noun, place, and time senses.", "positions":

 [{"id": "79:31/q05/p1", "position": "Food or vegetation eaten by both people and animals.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī, Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Kashshāf, Rāzī, Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and Study Quran explicitly include both. Rāzī cites 16:10 and 80:25–32 and infers this scope from the later statement that it is provision for people and livestock. Al-Samīn treats marʿā as a verbal noun with passive-object sense applied metaphorically to people. Ālūsī reports restricting the literal base to animals before extending it to people. Asad reports Rāzī's metonymic sense of all edible herbal produce."}, {"id": "79:31/q05/p2", "position": "Grazed vegetation, pasture, or fodder for livestock.", "reasons": "Jishumī derives the name from livestock grazing and eating it. Al-Kashshāf, Rāzī, and Bayḍāwī note an original sense of the grazing place. Biqāʿī includes what is grazed, its place, and its season. Ālūsī lists fodder, the act of grazing, and place or time as possible senses, reports an alleged original place sense, but judges fodder best here. Ibn ʿĀshūr derives marʿā from raʿā, takes a verbal noun for its grazed object, and says literal grazing is livestock eating pasture, grass, and fresh fodder. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes possible verbal-noun, time, and place forms, favors what is grazed, and compares 87:4. Bursevī glosses it as pasture."}, {"id": "79:31/q05/p3", "position": "Plants or vegetal growth generally.", "reasons": "Muqātil says earth's plants come from it. Ṭabarī names plants, transmitting the same from al-Ḍaḥḥāk; Ibn Jurayj, as transmitted in al-Durr, says all plants and other growth. Elmalılı adds grasses, pastures, and cultivated growth. Study Quran reports an allusion to all plant life."}]}
{"id": "79:31/q06", "question": "How does grazing language apply to human provision?", "turns_on": "Whether the extension from livestock grazing to human food is metaphor, metonymy, or an a fortiori implication from provision for animals.", "positions": [{"id": "79:31/q06/p1", "position": "It is extended metaphorically from livestock grazing to people eating.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and Rāzī compare 'roam/graze and play' and the nartaʿ reading at 12:12. Al-Samīn describes a verbal noun with passive-object sense used metaphorically of people. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says this usage is familiar Arabic, compares shepherd and flock, and cites 20:54. Ālūsī reports al-Ṭībī's explicit metaphor: resurrection-deniers are yoked with beasts in worldly enjoyment and heedlessness of the afterlife."}, {"id": "79:31/q06/p2", "position": "The animal-pasture term extends to human food by metonymy.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this account as an alternative to explicit metaphor. Asad attributes to Rāzī a metonymic reference to all edible herbal produce for humans or animals."}, {"id": "79:31/q06/p3", "position": "Human fruits and grain are left implicit because God's provision for animals implies greater care for humans.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says 79:33 signals the ellipsis and explains the inference from animal pasture to human food."}]}
{"id": "79:31/q07", "question": "How does bringing out water and pasture relate to the earth's spreading and the sequence of creation?", "turns_on": "How daḥāhā in the preceding verse is understood, and when the emergence of water and pasture occurs relative to creation of heaven and earth.", "positions": [{"id": "79:31/q07/p1", "position": "Earth existed before the sky, but its spreading after the sky brought its latent contents into actuality.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation and prefers the reading chosen by Ibn Jarīr. Ibn ʿAbbās says spreading brought forth water and pasture, split rivers, and placed mountains, sands, roads, and hills."}, {"id": "79:31/q07/p2", "position": "Spreading means preparing earth to produce provisions, an aptitude attained only after heaven existed.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports this alternative interpretation, comparing heaven to a father and earth to a mother."}, {"id": "79:31/q07/p3", "position": "After heaven and earth were created together and separated, spreading and bringing out water and pasture were later developmental stages.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī distinguishes daḥāhā, spreading or expanding earth, from creating it; he says water, pasture, and mountains appeared in later stages, and cites 21:30 and 79:32."}, {"id": "79:31/q07/p4", "position": "Some understand the adjacent 'spreading' as making earth spherical like an ostrich egg.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī reports this comparison without adopting it."}]}
{"id": "79:31/q08", "question": "How are 'earth' and 'mountains' parsed in the surrounding construction?", "turns_on": "The case reading of the surrounding nouns and whether later predicates explain omitted verbs.", "positions": [{"id": "79:31/q08/p1", "position": "Both are accusative through omitted verbs explained by later predicates.", "reasons": "Rāzī gives this parsing of the surrounding clauses."}, {"id": "79:31/q08/p2", "position": "Both are nominative subjects.", "reasons": "Rāzī records al-Ḥasan's reading with both nouns nominative."}]}
{"id": "79:31/q09", "question": "How do the earth's provisions serve the sūra's argument about resurrection?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:31/q09/p1", "position": "Making the earth habitable and providing for its creatures displays God's power to resurrect humanity.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says the sūra establishes resurrection and gathering and humanity's final fate, after preceding sūras' exposition; its oaths mark a decisive climax. He also points to recurring night and day as daily demonstrations: restoring life is no harder than creating humanity from nothing. Kur'an Yolu says the ordered cosmos confronts resurrection-deniers and cites 40:57, which makes creation of heaven and earth greater than creation of humanity; furnishing earth with provision for people and animals reinforces the argument."}]}
{"id": "79:31/q10", "question": "May Qur'anic writing or water used to wash it be consumed?", "turns_on": "Whether contact with internal impurity bars drinking washed-off writing, and whether drinking wash-water, swallowing the paper, and eating inscribed food receive distinct treatment.", "positions": [{"id": "79:31/q10/p1", "position": "One may not drink water used to wash Qur'anic writing, because it meets internal impurity.", "reasons": "An unnamed shaykh gives the prohibition and its ground, as reported by al-Burhān."}, {"id": "79:31/q10/p2", "position": "One may drink that wash-water; impurity in its original bodily location has no legal consequence.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān's author objects to the shaykh's impurity argument. Al-ʿImād al-Nihy permits washing a written Qur'anic scrap and drinking the water; the author saw this statement in Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ's hand."}, {"id": "79:31/q10/p3", "position": "The written paper itself must not be swallowed.", "reasons": "Al-ʿImād al-Nihy distinguishes swallowing the paper from drinking water in which its writing was washed."}, {"id": "79:31/q10/p4", "position": "Foods bearing some Qur'anic writing may be eaten.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports this allowance from al-Qāḍī al-Ḥusayn and al-Rāfiʿī."}, {"id": "79:31/q10/p5", "position": "A man ate a paper bearing the basmala out of reverence and then received wisdom in a dream.", "reasons": "Al-Bayhaqī transmits from al-Sulamī the story of Manṣūr ibn ʿAmmār; the note reports an event rather than a general legal ruling."}]}
{"id": "79:33/q01", "question": "What does matāʿ mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:33/q01/p1", "position": "Benefit or enjoyment granted for use; the word can imply that the enjoyment lasts only a limited time.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, the exegetes reported by Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn al-Jawzi himself, al-Qurtubi, and Ibn Abbas as reported by al-Suyuti gloss it as benefit. Ibn al-Jawzi's report illustrates benefit with uninhabited houses sheltering visitors from heat and cold. Ibn Ashur adds the limited duration of use and compares 7:24."}]}
{"id": "79:33/q02", "question": "How is matāʿ read at this point?", "turns_on": "Whether the word is accusative in the common reading or nominative as a new clause.", "positions": [{"id": "79:33/q02/p1", "position": "A nominative matāʿ is also possible, beginning a new clause.", "reasons": "Al-Farra says matāʿ lakum may begin a new clause with an omitted nominative element and cites comparable wording at 46:35 and 16:117; al-Nahhas reports his allowance of the nominative."}, {"id": "79:33/q02/p2", "position": "The common reading has accusative matāʿan.", "reasons": "Al-Samin calls the accusative the common reading and explains its two possible syntactic roles."}]}
{"id": "79:33/q03", "question": "What grammatical role does matāʿan have?", "turns_on": "Whether the accusative marks purpose, depends on an implicit verb, or follows a suppressed preposition; al-Farra also allows a nominative clause.", "positions": [{"id": "79:33/q03/p1", "position": "It is an accusative expression of purpose: God made these things for people and livestock to enjoy.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj relates the purpose to bringing out water and pasture. Al-Samin gives the purpose object as one analysis of the common accusative. Al-Alusi reports it and says that an objection based on the deniers addressed is answered because the address generalizes to humankind; he questions the premise that only believers benefit. Al-Qurtubi's alternative with an omitted preposition likewise expresses 'for you to enjoy it,' but specifies a different construction."}, {"id": "79:33/q03/p2", "position": "It is an accusative verbal noun governed by an omitted verb such as 'We provided you enjoyment.'", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi supplies 'I provide enjoyment'; al-Samin supplies mattaʿakum; Ibn Ashur supplies 'We provided you with provision.' Al-Alusi reports either an emphatic verbal noun for an omitted verb or a verbal noun licensed by the preceding actions' meaning of providing enjoyment. Al-Alusi rejects

the claim that this analysis by itself avoids the purpose objection, since it still states a purpose."}, {"id": "79:33/q03/p3", "position": "Matāʿ is nominative in a fresh clause with an omitted nominative element.", "reasons": "Al-Farra accepts matāʿ lakum as a new clause, adducing 46:35 and 16:117; al-Nahhas transmits his nominative analysis."}, {"id": "79:33/q03/p4", "position": "Its accusative follows an omitted preposition, yielding 'for you to enjoy it.'", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi offers this as an alternative to construing the word as a verbal noun governed by an omitted verb."}]}
{"id": "79:33/q04", "question": "Does 'you' limit the intended beneficiaries to the people directly addressed?", "turns_on": "Whether the wording restricts benefit to believers or extends the addressed provision to all people.", "positions": [{"id": "79:33/q04/p1", "position": "The immediate address is to those present, but its provision extends generally to humankind.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi replies that a direct address can have a general ruling and questions the claim that only believers are intended beneficiaries."}, {"id": "79:33/q04/p2", "position": "Only believers are the intended beneficiaries, despite the address to resurrection-deniers.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this as the premise of an objection to taking matāʿan as purpose; he counters that the ruling extends to humanity and calls the premise debatable."}]}
{"id": "79:33/q05", "question": "Which animals are meant by 'your livestock'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:33/q05/p1", "position": "Domestic livestock, including camels, cattle, and sheep.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi specifies these three kinds; Ibn Kathir adds that such animals are used for eating and riding."}]}
{"id": "79:33/q06", "question": "What enjoyment is provided for people and livestock?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:33/q06/p1", "position": "God makes the ordered earth and its resources useful as food, shelter, and other benefits for people and livestock.", "reasons": "Muqatil identifies pasture and other livelihood. Al-Farra, al-Qushayri, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, and al-Nasafi explain the acts as providing enjoyment. Al-Zajjaj and al-Alusi name water and pasture; al-Nahhas transmits al-Farra's benefit gloss. Ibn Kathir details springs, hidden resources, rivers, crops, trees, fruit, stabilizing mountains, eating, riding, and use until the allotted lifespan. Al-Biqai describes consumption followed by renewed supply. Al-Bursevi and al-Utbi include grass, trees, grain, fruit, salt obtained from water, and fire from green wood. Elmalili says spreading the crust makes earth habitable. Ibn Ashur adds that earth and mountains furnish use, shelter from enemies, and safe pasture, while the two lams reinforce the verbal noun. Al-Tabatabai relates heaven and earth's ordering to human and animal sustenance. The Study Quran adds that God sustains all things and makes them serve humans, citing 80:32, 22:65, 31:20, and 45:13."}]}
{"id": "79:33/q07", "question": "How does provision for people and livestock explain the preceding mention of pasture?", "turns_on": "Whether pasture itself covers human food or human food is implied by an inference from God's care for animals.", "positions": [{"id": "79:33/q07/p1", "position": "Pasture broadly includes or stands for all earthly products consumed by people and animals.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says the later provision for both proves pasture means everything both eat. Al-Bursevi treats grazing figuratively as everything consumed from earth, even salt from water and fire from green wood. Al-Utbi, reported by al-Bursevi, calls water and pasture a comprehensive expression embracing grass, trees, grain, fruit, salt, and fire."}, {"id": "79:33/q07/p2", "position": "Pasture names animal provision, while human fruits and grain are understood by a stronger inference.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says that if God cares for animals, people deserve care all the more, and 79:33 signals the omission of explicit fruits and grain."}]}
{"id": "79:33/q08", "question": "Why are people named before livestock?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:33/q08/p1", "position": "Rational beings take precedence over other creatures in the order of mention.", "reasons": "Al-Suyuti compares Gabriel's precedence over Michael and cites the ordering of creatures in glorification at 22:18."}]}
{"id": "79:33/q09", "question": "What does the verse imply about the purpose of God's acts?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:33/q09/p1", "position": "Divine action has purposes and benefits; making a habitable world and providing life are wise acts.", "reasons": "Al-Razi reports that advocates of purposes behind God's acts and rulings cite this verse. Elmalili argues that making earth livable is purposeful rather than futile or accidental, and that life has wisdom and an end."}]}
{"id": "79:33/q10", "question": "How do these provisions contribute to the proof of resurrection?", "turns_on": "The sources use created power, observable renewal, and divine wisdom as grounds for resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "79:33/q10/p1", "position": "Creating and ordering the greater world shows God's ability to recreate human beings after death.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi says preserving created substances allows their restoration after destruction. Al-Razi says creation proves resurrection rationally before 79:34 announces it. Al-Biqai places this within the surah's purpose of establishing gathering and final fate, with decisive oaths after earlier surahs' exposition. Bint al-Shati says the heavens, earth, water, pasture, and mountains make resurrection of decayed humans no hardship. Al-Tabatabai adds that the greater creation removes difficulty. Islahi says creating the heavens, earth, night, day, and sustenance establishes divine power. Kuran Yolu points to the vast ordered cosmos and cites 40:57, then specifically adduces earth's habitability and provision. The Study Quran likewise identifies creation's wonders as evidence of resurrection."}, {"id": "79:33/q10/p2", "position": "Recurring renewal of earthly life and provisions illustrates restoration and resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Biqai calls the daily return of night and day a demonstration of resurrection: restoring life is no harder than initial creation. He also points to the recurring cycle of consuming and replacing needed provision."}, {"id": "79:33/q10/p3", "position": "The wise provision of human sustenance entails an end beyond present life.", "reasons": "Islahi says God's power makes re-creation possible and His wisdom requires it; Elmalili adds that useful, purposeful life has wisdom and an end."}]}
{"id": "79:33/q11", "question": "What response do God's provisions call for from people?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize gratitude and worship, and one also draws a duty to share from human vicegerency.", "positions": [{"id": "79:33/q11/p1", "position": "People should recognize, thank, fear, and worship the Lord who provides for them.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says gratitude is embedded in the proof and invites exclusive worship; he also identifies a blend-then-division figure. Al-Tabatabai says creation and provision obligate knowledge, fear, and thanks. Asad cites the food passage 80:24-32 for awareness of God as Provider. Bint al-Shati says divine gifts recall the heedless, deniers, and arrogant to gratitude. The Study Quran also calls for thanks."}, {"id": "79:33/q11/p2", "position": "People should share these resources with all creatures.", "reasons": "The Study Quran relates sharing to the human role as God's vicegerents and cites 2:30, 6:165, and 35:39."}]}
{"id": "79:33/q12", "question": "How does mention of worldly enjoyment rebuke resurrection-deniers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:33/q12/p1", "position": "It likens deniers who enjoy this world and forget the next to cattle.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevi explains the rebuke through their absorption in worldly provision and neglect of the afterlife."}]}
